title: Strengthening Surge Capacity: Table-Top Exercise Focused on Protracted Conflict | All About the Base
transcriptText:
Would the United States be able to help
Taiwan defend itself in the event of a
Chinese invasion? The war in Ukraine and
the campaign against Iran have laid bare
a stark reality. The United States
severely struggles to observe production
to meet its national security needs.
Several war games spelling out potential
Chinese aggression in the Taiwan Strait
and an American-led military response
have also revealed significant
constraints on US manufacturing. Indeed,
in the most optimistic outcome of a
Chinese invasion of Taiwan, a CSIS war
game estimated that America and its
allies would lose 290 combat aircraft
and 24 ships after 4 weeks of
hostilities. How does the United States
quickly rebuild these programs and break
the cycle of vulnerability?
In a recent tabletop exercise, I our
team at CSIS measured the industrial
resources America and its allies needed
to succeed in a prolonged conflict
against China.
In US defense and industrial planning,
much emphasis has traditionally been
placed on whether the United States
holds the military capabilities, such as
munitions, ships, and aircraft required
to deter and if and if necessary prevail
in short conflicts. Yet, the wars in
Ukraine and Iran show that fighting
could be protracted. Does the United
States have the industrial capacity
to coordinate between government and
industry, scale manufacturing with
allies, and surge defense production
when needed?
To discuss these subjects and the
intersection of US production capacity
and national security, we'll be speaking
with my colleague, Professor Mark
Cancian, senior advisor with the defense
and security department here at CSIS,
and the lead for our recent
manufacturing security tabletop
exercise. As usual, I'm your host, Jerry
McGinn, and welcome back to another
episode of All About the Base.
Mark, it's really great to have you on
the show. Great to have you here.
Well, thanks for having me on the
program.
Uh as you know, we've been conducting a
study for the Pentagon on that focuses
on identifying key elements necessary
for a manufacturing security program to
help surge production uh of munitions.
One of the key components of this effort
was a tabletop exercise, which you led,
uh and it drew on a series of 70 war
games that you have run over the past 3
years. First, could you describe uh the
the war games that provided the
foundation for this TTX?
Sure. Yeah, we ran about 70 day-long war
games in three projects. The first one
looked at a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.
>> Mhm. Uh second one looked at an invasion
with nuclear weapons. And the third
looked at blockades, different blockade
scenarios.
And what we found from the invasion
scenario was that the United States
could sustain a democratic and
autonomous Taiwan with the help of its
coalition partners, but it would come at
very high cost uh to both the United
States, its
uh coalition partners, and the the
Chinese. Mhm.
But missing from these three sets of war
games was insights into what a
protracted campaign might look like and
what it might demand.
By the fourth week, we got some insights
into that as both sides started to run
low on munitions. For some of them, the
United States ran out after a single
week. And they began to fight
differently because the lack of
munitions was constraining them. And
that was one reason why this new project
was so interesting, because it gave some
insight into what would be needed for a
protracted conflict that went beyond the
4 weeks that we had looked at.
So, Mark, can you describe the
underlying concept behind the TTX that
we ran?
Yeah, the TTX uh had three phases, as
you can see up here. We gathered
uh groups of people. We had three groups
that had uh people from industry, people
from government, people from
uh think tanks, and bringing them
together to see if uh they could come up
with some new ideas for protracted
conflict. We had three uh
uh phases to this. We'll talk about that
in in a second. The scenario was the
basic uh Chinese invasion of Taiwan, but
an invasion that goes on for several
months, not just a couple of weeks. Let
me have the second piece up.
And here are the three phases.
The first phase was
what would industry and government do
when the war begins? What actions can
they take to sustain and enhance the
forces?
The second was
uh took them to day 60. In other words,
both sides have used a lot of munitions.
The United States has taken a lot of
losses. So, what do you do then when it
looks now like this conflict might be
protracted?
And then, the third phase, we brought
them back to the beginning again and
said, "Okay, now that you've looked at
what hap- what you might do at the
beginning, what you might do at day 60,
what do you recommend that we do today
in the real world to prepare for this
kind of situation?" Mhm.
So, what was the major outcome and
takeaway from the TTX? Within the TTX,
uh there was an industrial mobilization
gap between months 3 and 12 of the
crisis. What made this gap significant?
Yeah, let me have the next slide.
Okay, and the next one.
In months 1 and 2, uh the US can draw
down some of its existing inventories.
Of course, we have some with the forces,
but you can see here some of the other
uh pools of equipment that are out there
that we can draw on, and that will keep
the forces going a month, maybe 2
months, up to full strength or
essentially.
Let me have the second piece.
But we uh when you get out to month 12,
then you have uh industry starting to
produce new equipment, new munitions,
and there were many s- suggestions,
recommendations about how we might
enhance that. The problem is, let me
have the final
is the gap between month 2 and month 12.
In other words, after you've run out of
all the equipment that you already have
in the inventory pools you have, but
before industry can start kicking out
some surge production, what do you do?
And that was the most difficult uh
thing to talk to think about, because
it's not something that we customarily
discuss.
What was a lesson you took away from
American and allied industrial
production? Okay, next one.
What we did was to look at what
government should do, what industry
might do,
and what foreign partners might do, to
see all the different pieces and where
we might strengthen preparations today.
Mhm. So, one of the things was to
develop some sort of mechanism for
coordinating industry. It became clear
that you would have to have companies
talking with each other,
and to do that in a way that wasn't
constrained by like antitrust um uh
legislation. So, in the past, World War
One, World War Two, we had production
boards like this. We would need some
mechanism on call uh that we could use.
Waiting until the war began to divi-
develop this would be too late, cuz it
would take weeks to get it going, and
you know, then we'd be way behind. Next
one.
There's been a lot of talk about uh
strategic reserves.
The uh there have been some discussion
about having a reserve of chips. Mhm.
The problem with chips is that they're
out of date in 12 months. So, it doesn't
make any sense to build a reserve. What
you what you will need to do in an
emergency is have the ability to divert
chips from the private sector, and the
Defense Production Act provides those
capabilities. Uh but we might want to
build a reserve of rare earth, so that
industry can immediately go to that
before we have to start diverting from
the civilian economy. Mhm. Next one.
And the the third one is to bring
defense industry in very quickly, to
have uh the heads of industry meet with
the secretary and the president,
to let them know what the government's
plan is, and to give them some
confidence that they can go on risk and
take some actions to enhance the surge
production, and that the government will
uh protect them. This is where a
mechanism like the war like a modern-day
war production board would be helpful.
Exactly, yes.
There were a few other things that could
help. One of them was having legislation
ready to justify the war and provide
Congress with an opportunity to uh
support the effort. Uh this was also uh
stated by industry, that they wanted to
have some uh demand signal
>> Yeah, some some confidence that the war
effort would be supported in Congress,
and that they would then uh provide also
the resources. Next one.
Emergency funding that Congress has been
pretty good about this whenever uh we've
been in a conflict and the executive
branch asked for money, uh Congress has
been pretty good about providing it. The
executive branch just has to have those
mechanisms ready to go. Again, they
can't spend 2 or 3 weeks putting an
emergency supplemental together.
Next one.
And finally, it's helpful in the
contracting documents if there are
provisions for surge. They may never be
used, but having those in there again
speeds the process up. You don't spend 2
weeks renegotiating a a contract before
you can surge production.
Specific to the Taiwan Strait, what
capabilities and industrial inputs were
most important for American allied
forces to respond to potential Chinese
aggressions? What munitions and
platforms were the hardest to produce
once they had been lost in combat? Uh
one thing that industry talked about was
the need to surge the workforce. And
that's difficult because often you're
looking for uh skilled laborers.
The idea has come up about, you know,
some sort of uh
reserve corps of uh industrial workers.
That's not really feasible. Uh you don't
have the mechanisms like with our
reservist. Uh but what you can do is is
have provisions ready to provide signing
bonuses and uh reemployment rights for
anyone who comes into the industry to
enhance the provide incentives for
people to come in and provide that surge
workforce. Next one.
So, machinery is often a bottleneck and
it's difficult for industry itself to
have a lot of machinery that's standing
around and not used year after year. One
possibility was to identify machinery in
the civilian sector that uh
the defense industrial base might use in
an emergency. Uh
you can see some of the example examples
here. That way we can leverage the
civilian industry without the cost of
having unproductive resources hanging
around. Yeah, Congress actually uh put
in the last appropriations act provision
for civil reserve manufacturing network,
which essentially gets to some of this
issue. Good. Exactly. Next one.
And then resilience in the industrial
base. Many people pointed out that cyber
could be uh a problem. It's a problem
now even in peacetime and in wartime
they'd be facing, for example, a a
Chinese uh cyber onslaught and they
needed to have the defenses uh ready to
go uh so that they weren't disrupted at
the critical moment.
And last one.
And this was something new. It's
something new uh
for uh the military in the United
States. And
what it is is hardening against
un- unmanned aerial systems. Because
what we've seen in Ukraine and in Iran
is that adversaries can sneak drone
systems into the country and at the
beginning of a conflict let those go
uh and have them fly up on to airbases
or even industrial facilities and cause
a lot of destruction when they're not
prepared for it.
Much harder to do later in a conflict
when people are ready, but on that first
day, we saw in Ukraine again in in Iran,
it could be very devastating. So,
they'll need to have some um some
hardening and it could just be as simple
as putting doors on facilities and
making sure that there's no easy way to
get in.
One of the questions you asked was what
are the most critical munitions or what
is difficult to produce. There are two
kinds of munitions that are critical.
One is long-range precision fire against
ground targets and the other is air and
missile defense. Uh on both of those
>> Tomahawk and Patriot, yeah. Exactly. In
the first category would be like
Tomahawk. It would be uh JASSM. And in
the second category it would be THAAD,
Patriot, SM-3s.
The United States is low on those now
uh because of the conflict in Iran
uh and therefore is working very hard to
rebuild those muni- those inventories.
And they're important uh
for a couple of reasons. For the ground
attack, it's important because
US platforms, at least in the early days
of a conflict, need to stand back. They
can't get too close to Chinese defensive
zone. The Chinese have a lot of missiles
and if you get too close, you'll be um
hit with these missiles. So, standing
back, having long-range missiles that
can shoot in, very important.
Uh and for air and missile defense, of
course, the Chinese have thousands of
missiles and our air and missile
defenses on places like Guam, like
Okinawa, uh potentially on Taiwan or
mainland Japan, again, are critical to
defend our facilities against those
attacks. And these are
exactly the systems that are that take a
long time to build uh and
you know, that we don't have enough of.
Concerning
America's allies and partners, what
opportunities exist for the US to source
key platforms from foreign stocks,
co-produce with foreign manufacturers,
and use allies as, you know, surge
repair depots?
Well, this is very important because in
a crisis like this, in a conflict that
goes on for a while, the US industrial
base is going to be working as hard as
it can, but that's not going to be quite
enough. We need the help of allies and
and partners. And that's not something
we do very easily. Why don't you give me
the first bullet?
One possibility is to buy systems from
our allies and partners, either systems
that we've sold to them that we would
now buy back, like like Patriot, or some
systems that they have that uh
might work with our platforms, but that
we haven't in the past uh used
extensively.
Uh that would be both of these would be
ways to expand our inventories of
munitions
without having to wait for new
production. Why don't you give me the
next one?
Diverting foreign military sales, we're
doing that now as a result of the war in
Iran. Of course, it's difficult for many
of our allies and partners who are
counting on these munitions, but we will
likely have to do some triage here,
allowing sales to go through for, in
this case, Taiwan or Japan or uh
Australia, but maybe pulling back some
from other parts of of the world uh and
not telling them they can't have it, but
putting them back in the line until uh
the conflict is over.
And give me the next one.
And this has a lot of potential. Repair
forward.
Our allies and partners have
shipyards that can do repairs. They have
aircraft facilities that can do repairs.
One of the things that is hard to
uh project is
uh the amount of battle damage that our
systems, ships, aircraft will sustain.
I was talking to uh the head of Air
Force depot maintenance couple years ago
and he said that at the height of the
Vietnam War there was a 1-year backlog
of aircraft maintenance
because of the war. Uh and this would be
a way to get around that and to do it
forward so that it's aircraft ships
could be repaired and then sent right
back into battle. That seems to be one
of the premises of the regional
sustainment framework which DOD is
looking to establish as well. It it it
seems to be a key component of AUKUS as
well. So, that that's great to hear.
What did the TTX reveal about the main
challenges involved in international
industrial collaboration, Mark?
Once the conflict begins, it's too late
then to be thinking about how to surge
production and to increase inventories
because it takes several years for those
systems to be delivered.
The United States has to be thinking
about that ahead of time and
particularly this gap that we talked
about at the very beginning. The
solutions in there are just not very
comfortable.
Very easy to talk about how we would
surge defense industry.
Easy to talk about how we would draw
down existing inventories, but the idea
of going to allies and partners and
buying things back from them, maybe
buying different kinds of systems,
maybe like low-cost drones, for example,
which we're already building.
Things that need to be done in that gap
are critical, but also a bit
uncomfortable because that's not the way
the acquisition system is designed.
Thanks so much, Mark, for your
tremendous insights into this issue.
Uh today's discussion on manufacturing
security and its impact on the national
on our national security demonstrates
the scope of our work here at the Center
for the Industrial Base. Mapping and
addressing our industrial
vulnerabilities at home is essential to
provide for the defense of our allies
and national interests abroad. Thanks so
much for watching and we look forward to
seeing you again soon. And remember,
it's all about the base.
